raw_text:
Angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibition (ARNI) was developed to augment endogenous natriuretic-peptide signaling while maintaining renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system blockade. The clinical path was shaped by dual ACE–neprilysin inhibition: omapatrilat improved functional and biomarker measures versus lisinopril in IMPRESS but failed to beat enalapril convincingly in OVERTURE and raised concern about angioedema, plausibly from concomitant bradykinin and substance-P accumulation [1,2]. Sacubitril/valsartan avoided ACE inhibition by pairing the neprilysin inhibitor prodrug sacubitril with valsartan; PARADIGM-HF was therefore designed as an active-comparator mortality–morbidity trial against evidence-based enalapril rather than placebo [3].

In PARADIGM-HF, 8442 ambulatory patients with symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), elevated natriuretic peptides, and tolerance of run-in enalapril and sacubitril/valsartan had a 20% relative reduction in cardiovascular death or heart-failure hospitalization, a 20% reduction in cardiovascular death, and a 16% reduction in all-cause mortality with sacubitril/valsartan [4]. Secondary analyses supported clinical coherence: ARNI reduced progression among survivors, including intensification of therapy, emergency visits, and hospitalization [5], and reduced both sudden death and death from worsening heart failure [6]. Benefit was broadly consistent across age and baseline systolic blood pressure, although symptomatic hypotension was more frequent, especially in lower-pressure patients [7,8]. Importantly, advantages persisted after dose reduction, among clinically stable patients without recent decompensation, and when recurrent heart-failure hospitalizations were counted rather than only first events [9-11].

Safety and comorbidity analyses refined implementation. Sacubitril/valsartan slowed estimated glomerular filtration rate decline versus enalapril despite modestly increasing albuminuria [12]. It lowered severe hyperkalemia risk among patients receiving mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists [13] and improved glycemic control in patients with diabetes [14]. Health-status analyses showed less deterioration in physical and social limitations [15]. Biomarker work linked reductions in NT-proBNP to improved outcomes, establishing NT-proBNP—not BNP—as the preferred marker for monitoring response because BNP is a neprilysin substrate and may rise early after initiation [16].

Translation from trial to practice required titration and acute-care data. TITRATION showed that gradual up-titration was feasible, particularly in patients naive to or on low-dose ACE inhibitor/ARB therapy [17]. PIONEER-HF then demonstrated that in-hospital initiation after stabilization for acute decompensated HFrEF reduced NT-proBNP more than enalapril without excess renal dysfunction, hyperkalemia, symptomatic hypotension, or angioedema [18]. Biomarker substudies showed early favorable effects on high-sensitivity troponin, soluble ST2, and urinary cGMP [19], and efficacy appeared consistent across achieved dose levels [20]. TRANSITION showed that initiation before discharge or within 14 days after discharge was similarly feasible, with about half achieving target dose by 10 weeks [21].

Mechanistic and remodeling studies provided additional support but should not be overinterpreted as outcomes trials. PROVE-HF, an open-label single-arm study, associated NT-proBNP reduction after sacubitril/valsartan initiation with reverse remodeling, including improved left ventricular ejection fraction and reduced ventricular volumes [22]. EVALUATE-HF did not significantly improve aortic characteristic impedance versus enalapril at 12 weeks, but did show favorable changes in some remodeling indices [23]. These studies reinforce biological plausibility while leaving clinical outcomes anchored primarily in PARADIGM-HF and PIONEER-HF.

Evidence is more nuanced in heart failure with preserved or mildly reduced ejection fraction. PARAMOUNT, a phase 2 HFpEF trial, reduced NT-proBNP versus valsartan and suggested favorable atrial remodeling [24], with renal analyses suggesting slower eGFR decline [25]. PARAGON-HF narrowly missed statistical significance for its primary composite of total heart-failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death versus valsartan, but suggested benefit in patients with lower ejection fraction and in women [26]. A pooled PARADIGM-HF/PARAGON-HF analysis showed a treatment gradient across ejection fraction, with greatest benefit below the preserved range and attenuation at higher ejection fractions [27]. PARALLAX reduced NT-proBNP but did not improve 6-minute walk distance at 24 weeks [28]. Thus, ARNI is foundational in HFrEF and selected HFmrEF, while HFpEF use is individualized.

Limits remain. LIFE did not show superiority of sacubitril/valsartan over valsartan in advanced HFrEF and highlighted tolerability challenges in very ill patients [29]. In PARADISE-MI, early post–myocardial infarction sacubitril/valsartan did not significantly reduce cardiovascular death or incident heart failure compared with ramipril [30]. Overall, sacubitril/valsartan represents a major advance for chronic and stabilized acute HFrEF, best used early, titrated pragmatically, and integrated with beta-blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and SGLT2 inhibitors.
